what_it_does: NOR flash is a type of storage chip used in tiny microcontrollers (the sort that run a smart lock or a sensor node) because it allows reading arbitrary bytes quickly and cheaply. Managing files on NOR flash requires software that tracks where data is stored and spreads writes evenly across the chip to prevent any one area from wearing out — a job called wear leveling. Existing file system software borrowed ideas from larger storage systems, dividing the flash into small logical blocks and tracking each one individually, which means even a small change can trigger many tiny bookkeeping writes and sometimes a full scan of the entire device — wasting precious time and causing far more actual writes than logically necessary. This paper redesigns the entire storage software stack to work at a coarser grain that matches how NOR flash naturally erases (in larger chunks), merges the bookkeeping layers that were previously separate, and thereby slashes the ratio of actual storage writes to the useful data written.
